en: He is a man who would bring.
As huge as half a mountain,
As though he would devour a soul he met,
Steel-clawed, stone-hearted—
Where has this fierce brute come from?
In what place was he born?
He will throw the world into uproar.
He is a keen hero and skillful;
He is strong enough to shake the world.
Worthy of all the world's people,
He has the look of a mighty man;
Ready to assault the world,
He has the look of a champion.
When turning his spear to strike,
He has the look of a skillful man;
Raising dust throughout the world,
He has the look of a mighty man.
Ruling a people, knowing his folk,
Perhaps he is one of the able heroes;
Never turning back from death,
Perhaps he is one of the mighty warriors.
Bringing good fortune if sent ahead,
His blue-maned courage shows.
Seeing him here, now
My thoughts are deeply stirred.
He is a champion, he is a lion;
He is a hero surpassing mortals.
If we had sheep, sharing a fold,
If we ate food, sharing a feast,
If we camped together at a chosen place,
He looks to be one of the champions.
If we met face to face and became friends,
Keeping treasure, gathering it together,
If we died, sharing the same faith,
If we were heroes, joining our strength,
If we entered slaughter, sharing one wish—
A riverside camp, a broad open slope,
Could it be a place we could not settle?
Sharing one faith together,
Could he be a man who would not join me!”
Seeing Bakay and marveling,
The blue-maned one stood thinking:
“Whose battle cry is his, what is his origin?
Who are his forebears, which is his village?
Born in Kakan-Chin,
Is he a cunning one come from the Kalmyks?
Is his faith the faith of Islam,
Is he one of the Muslims?
His heroism is extraordinary;
His prowess is immense.
He is distinguished, he is a support;
He is a lion surpassing mortals;
He is a khan, huge as a mountain.
Annihilating those who face him,
He has the look of a resourceful man.
What is this man who has come before me?
No such son arises in the world.
His figure and his bearing,
The way he sits his horse—
He has a tulpar beneath him;
A mighty fellow, a skilled spearman.
He is keen, he is a lion;
He is an exceedingly brave hero.
Choosing a tulpar beneath him,
Perhaps he is one of the heroes who ride,
Traversing the whole earth,
Roaming all the world,
Finding no mountain to crash against,
Finding no enemy to fight,
Perhaps he is one of the heroes who roam.
Taking the road on a six-month journey,
Never growing weary beneath me,
If only he could become my swift steed!
This person who has come before me,
To generous Lord Manas,
A friend into the next world—
If only he could become my kinsman!
As a kinsman, by my side,
Will he stand close and true?
If by chance he is an enemy,
Will he shout and thrust his spear?
Jousting midway between us,
Will God utterly strike us down?
If he is kin to this soul,
I shall offer words blessed by Khizir;
If by chance he is an enemy,
I shall thrust my spear without mercy.
Fighting him one against one,
Let me put my courage to the test;
Thrusting my spear without fleeing,
Let me face him once and die!
The world's four corners
He has circled four times.
He is one of the mighty warriors,
Girded with an unsheathed sword.
His courage is great, his wrath fierce;
He has the bearing of a seasoned man,
Of one who would stand as your support,
The bearing of a far-seeing man.
Standing against him one to one,
Fighting seven days without rest,
Let me make a splendid contest.
If he is a warrior skilled with the spear,
Let me meet my death;
If he is truly a friend,
Let me draw close to him.
Staring at Bakay in wonder,
Lion Manas was astonished.
Without getting an answer to “Who are you?”
Unable to tell friend from foe,
On the ridge of Oluya-Ata,
Along the gray hills,
He saw a mountainlike man on the plain,
He saw a khan endowed with sacred power.
Then blood-stained Manas the lion,
Seeing Bakay, stared in wonder.
“Is this man friend or foe?” he wondered,
He stared, dumbfounded with astonishment.
He is a great lord and a lion;
Among mortals none like him can be found.
Where has this warrior come from?
Drenching blood with blood,
If by chance he is an enemy,
Let me stand and fight without fleeing;
If the Creator's decree
Falls upon my neck, let me face it.
Grappling by the hems,
Clashing with thunderous blows,
Let me fight to the end.
If he is a fine, strong warrior,
Let me face him in battle.
Your Manas saw Bakay,
Unable to tell whether he was friend,
Unable to tell whether he was foe,
Staring dumbfounded in astonishment,
He reined in prancing Akkula,
Turning his head aside.
Khan Manas stood amazed,
Toward the saddle-shaped pass
He now stood looking.
On a horse like a blue-gray winged steed,
In a robe of blue ribbed cloth,
Along a winding, narrow trail,
Turning aside in no direction,
He came steadily, unconcerned,
Not reckoning blood-stained Manas on the road
Worth even the hem of his trousers.
Poised like a hawk,
With a golden-cheeked battle-axe
Hung upon his bare forearm,
Wearing gray deerskin trousers,
Taking on a gray tiger's aspect,
His gray deerskin trousers
Trimmed with strands of gold,
With the skin of a whole otter
Fastened to each trouser leg.
In Bakay's right hand
Was a golden-cheeked battle-axe;
At the wolf-man's left side
Was a gilded pouch.
He is awesome and a lion,
A lion and a warrior.
One could not dream this in sleep;
Even among marvels such things do not occur.
“His valor is of another kind,”
Manas stood saying.
“Where has this outstanding man come from?”
Manas stood bristling,
Looking ready to attack,
Preparing to thrust his painted spear.
Then leopard Bakay,
Who truly knew the ways of battle,
Lord Bakay the tiger
Also possessed alertness.
Resourceful and full of wisdom,
He also possessed foresight.
In thrusting and wielding the spear
He also possessed skill.
Fortunate beyond others and ingenious,
He also possessed strength.
Your elder Bakay, bringer of good fortune,
Put in the vanguard, was like a countless host;
He also possessed knowledge.
He had grown up alongside holy men,
Holy men had grown under his care;
He also possessed a spiritual master's gifts.
His speech was sweet, his words honey;
He also possessed eloquence.
He was the champion, he was the support,
Your champion Manas's companion.
For your elder, champion Bakay,
This was the place where they met.
He was the great lord, he was the khan;
His elder, old Bakay,
Was wisdom itself.
Wearing out horses, surveying the land,
Wandering through the world,
Seeking magnanimous Lord Manas,
This was the time when he arrived.
If you ask about all his ways,
He was born in a renowned place;
Against everyone who faced him
He had brought tumult.
Khan Bakay, Bay's son,
Who rinsed his mouth with honey,
Who rested his head against a throne,
Who wrapped his feet in yellow gold,
Who never drew back from death,
Who never retreated from an attacking foe,
His fierce presence like a countless host,
A lucky support for those who leaned on him,
Wise Bakay was a lion.
Hearing news of him from afar,
Hearing the report without delay,
“That slaughter broke out in Altay,
And he migrated away,” he heard.
Old Bakay stirred,
Departing in anger;
Then your elder Bakay,
Showing a lion's bearing,
Disappointed in many places,
Determined to migrate to Talas
And go there to become a companion.
Then he had sought out
Manas, Jakyp's son,
To settle his camp under his protection,
The youngest of the six lions,
To become a companion to Manas.
That Bakay, hearing his fame,
Sought your lion, blood-stained Manas,
To take him as his companion.
Once he had made the lord his companion,
The world's four corners
He would seek out and explore.
His elder, saintly Bakay,
Onto the saddle-shaped ridge,
Urging his blue-gray winged steed,
Your wolf-man now appeared.
Mounted on mountainlike Akkula,
His mind was drawn away;
Before him he appeared,
And when he appeared before him,
Your elder, leopard Bakay—
If I speak, my words are a plea to God—
Had one who foretold six months of hardship,
Profit and loss,
Death and suffering,
Who told him the truth:
Upon his right shoulder, speaking,
There was a naked child,
Who made known what was unknown,
Wise old Bakay,
Who made the unperceived perceptible,
Saintly Bakay the falcon,
Traversing the whole earth,
Through the wide world's shrines,
